name: Otto DIY Maker Kit
description: A small bipedal, mostly 3D-printed walking robot built around an Arduino Nano, 4 SG90 micro servos (2 hip, 2 ankle), and an HC-SR04 ultrasonic sensor doubling as its face. Programmed via "Otto Blockly" (a Blockly-derived block coding app that generates real Arduino C/C++) or directly in Arduino IDE/MicroPython. Sold either as a full kit with pre-printed body parts or an electronics-only "Maker Kit" for owners of their own 3D printer, who print the free, open STL files themselves. Descends from a documented lineage: Kevin Biagini's "BoB the Biped" → BQ's Zowi (Spain) → creator Camilo Parra Palacio's "Tito" → Otto, first launched via a 2017 Kickstarter.

specs.label: Battery
specs.note: Otto DIY+ and the newer HP Otto line switch to a rechargeable 3.7V Li-ion/LiPo pack instead

specs.label: Weight
specs.note: no official figure found in this research; weight would vary by 3D-print settings and electronics-only vs. full kit

specs.label: Dimensions
specs.note: assembled size per the Otto DIY project's own community documentation; an independent retailer listing gives a close ~11 × 6.5 × 11.5 cm

specs.label: Sensors
specs.note: obstacle avoidance/distance sensing; a passive buzzer provides sound; some variants add a MAX7219 LED matrix face or RGB LEDs

specs.label: Software
specs.note: Blockly-derived (Google/MIT lineage) block coding generates real compiled Arduino code; official MicroPython port and a mobile Bluetooth app also exist

specs.label: Control Board
specs.note: the current commercial "HP Otto" flagship has moved to an ESP32 (Wi-Fi/BLE) board instead — a separate, newer product line from the classic open Otto DIY described here

specs.label: Actuation
specs.note: 2 hip + 2 ankle, giving the biped walking gait; Otto DIY+ upgrades to MG90 metal-gear servos and adds Bluetooth

specs.label: Body
specs.note: press-fit, no supports needed at ~0.15mm layer height/20% infill; free STL files published on GitHub, Printables, and Thingiverse

specs.label: Kit Options
specs.note: a full "Builder Kit" ships pre-printed body parts; a cheaper electronics-only kit assumes you own a 3D printer and print the free body files yourself

specs.label: Age Range
specs.note: an independent review explicitly recommends against unsupervised assembly by elementary-age kids, citing dense wiring and delicate servo calibration — a real tension with the marketed age range

specs.label: Variants
specs.value: Basic, DIY+, Humanoid, Ninja, HP Otto
specs.note: this entry's photo matches the arm/gripper-equipped Humanoid-style build; HP Otto (2024, ESP32-based) is a separately-branded commercial line from Moravia Consulting under HP's brand license

sourcing: Specs and history compiled from Otto DIY's own site, blog, and software pages, the OttoDIY GitHub organization's repositories and their license files, Hackaday.io project pages for the original Otto and Otto DIY+, the original 2017 Kickstarter campaign page, HP Robots' current product/FAQ pages and reseller listings (Moravia Education, RobotShop, dstewart.com), and independent reviews (Tech Age Kids, mia-cat.com). Several details are flagged as unconfirmed above: the exact scope of what's open vs. proprietary in the newest HP Otto electronics, the "Kickstarter fraud" claim (one-sided, not independently corroborated), creator Camilo Parra Palacio's country of origin, and whether a Distributed Design Platform listing represents an actual won award or a nomination. A recollection that this project has documented Latin American humanitarian/institutional STEM adoption could not be independently confirmed and is likely a conflation with its Spain-based Zowi/BQ lineage; it isn't included above. This entry hasn't yet been cross-linked into the rest of the Classroom & Coding Kits subcategory or synced to the directory listing; that's planned for a later pass.

pricing.summary: Current HP-branded Otto kits run roughly **$150-$215** for a full Starter Builder Kit and around **$150** for the electronics-only Starter Creator Kit, with price varying by reseller. The original classic Builder Kit (**$49.99**) and Maker Kit (**$29.99**) are no longer officially produced, since Otto DIY's line has moved to this HP-branded product.

editorial.heading: Insights
editorial.body: The classic Otto DIY project is genuinely open source (GPL/MIT-licensed code, CC-BY-SA body files), but the newer commercial "HP Otto" line built by Moravia Consulting is narrower: the project's own blog states its custom electronics now balance openness with "product integrity protection" and reserve premium content for supporters and partners.
